nodes.label: Controller to Service to Repository Architecture
nodes.rationale: Business logic stays in Services and database access stays in Repositories so authorization and company-isolation checks live in exactly one layer and cannot be bypassed by a controller reaching into a repository directly.

nodes.label: Never Trust Client-Provided Ownership Fields
nodes.rationale: companyId, role, createdBy and verification flags are never read from the request because a client could escalate privilege or cross tenants by setting them; ownership must come from the authenticated user instead.

nodes.label: Company Isolation Rules
nodes.rationale: Query authorization is enforced at the service/repository level and never by frontend filtering, since a filtered UI still issues a reachable API call. Every company-owned entity needs a clear ownership path for this to be enforceable.

nodes.label: DTO Boundary Rules
nodes.rationale: Request DTOs carry only client-controlled information; backend-controlled fields are assigned by the service. companyId is deliberately omitted from recruiter/job creation requests when it can be derived from authentication, so there is no field to forge.

nodes.label: MapStruct Mapping with Ignored Backend Fields
nodes.rationale: MapStruct request mappings ignore id, role, company, password, createdAt, updatedAt, emailVerified and phoneNumberVerified so an incoming DTO cannot silently overwrite backend-owned state. Password encoding is kept in the service, not the mapper, so BCrypt is never skipped by a mapping path.

nodes.label: Password Handling Rules
nodes.rationale: Passwords are always BCrypt encoded, never logged, never placed in a JWT and never exposed in response DTOs, because a JWT is readable by anyone holding it and logs are a common exfiltration path.

nodes.label: Company Terminology Rule
nodes.rationale: 'Company' is mandated and 'Organization' is forbidden across database, entity and business vocabulary so naming stays searchable and mapping/repository method names line up with entity properties.

nodes.label: Repository Method Naming Must Match Entity Properties
nodes.rationale: Spring Data derives queries from method names, so existsByEmail is valid only if the entity has an email property; existsByCompanyEmail fails at context startup unless companyEmail genuinely exists. Uniqueness is additionally enforced at the database level, with service-level duplicate checks kept only for friendly error messages.

nodes.label: Minimal Change / No Unnecessary Abstraction Policy
nodes.rationale: Inspect before writing, reuse existing services, do not rewrite unrelated code and preserve existing API contracts, so incremental AI-assisted edits cannot quietly redesign the project or break consumers.
